title: Introduction to R
text:
R programming language
R first appeared in 1993. It is a programming language designed for working with data and statistics.
R is usually interpreted: we write commands and R runs them without a separate compile step.

2 + 2

[1] 4

title: Introduction to R
text:
Find your way around RStudio
R does the calculations. RStudio gives us places to write code and see what happened.


Source: write and save a script. This pane appears when you open a file.

Console: run commands and read their output or errors.

Environment: see objects created in the current R session.

Files, Plots, and Help: find files, see figures, and read documentation.

The panels can be arranged differently on your computer. Look for their names rather than their position.

title: Introduction to R
text:
What is an R Project?
An R Project is a folder for one piece of work, with a small .Rproj file that RStudio uses to reopen it.

Keep scripts, data, and results together.
Open the .Rproj file to return to the project.
Use paths relative to that folder so your code is easier to share.

Think of it as a home for the exercise.

title: Introduction to R
section: YOUR TURN Create your first project
text:
YOUR TURN Create your first project
In RStudio:

Choose File → New Project… → New Directory → New Project.
Name it practical and choose a folder you can find again.
Click Create Project. Check the project name at the top-right of RStudio.
Choose File → New File → R Script and save it as practice.R inside the project.

Use the Files panel to create folders called data and Results. The names and capital letters should match the examples.

title: Introduction to R
text:
A simple project layout
practical/
├── practical.Rproj
├── practice.R
├── data/
└── Results/
Save input files in data and things you create in Results. Bigger projects often have an R folder for scripts too.
The .Rproj file helps RStudio open the project. Your .R script contains the code you want to keep.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Write, run, save
Type 2 + 2 into practice.R, place the cursor on that line, and click Run. You can also use Ctrl+Enter on Windows/Linux or Cmd+Enter on Mac.
The command is sent to the Console and the answer appears there. Select several lines to run them together.

Saving stores your code in a file. Running asks R to execute it. Save and run after changing an example so the file and the result agree.
A Console > means R is ready. If you see +, it is usually waiting for something such as a closing bracket or quote; press Esc and check the command.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Use a function
A function does a job. Put the inputs, called arguments, inside its brackets:

ages <- c(23, 35, 41, 52)
mean(ages)

[1] 37.75

length(ages)

[1] 4


Missing values are written as NA. Some functions need us to decide how to handle them:

scores <- c(7, 8, NA)
mean(scores, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 7.5


Here, na.rm = TRUE asks mean() to leave missing values out of the calculation. Use ?mean in the Console to read its help page.

title: Introduction to R
section: You can write a function too
text:
You can write a function too

sumFun <- function(a, b) {
  a + b
}

sumFun(5, 6)

[1] 11


a and b are the inputs. The code between { and } says what to do with them.
For now, most of our work will use functions that other people have already written. You do not need to memorise how to write your own before continuing.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Packages in R
A package is a collection of functions, documentation, and sometimes data that people develop and share.
Many packages are distributed through CRAN, the Comprehensive R Archive Network. CRAN hosts packages and checks submitted updates; package authors maintain the packages themselves.
Install a package into your R library when you first need it:

install.packages("tibble")
# Or, if pak is installed:
pak::pkg_install("tibble")

You normally do not need to reinstall it each time you open RStudio.

title: Introduction to R
section: Load a package when you use it
text:
Load a package when you use it
library() makes a package’s functions available in the current session:

library(tibble)
tibble(a = 1)

# A tibble: 1 × 1
      a
  <dbl>
1     1


You can also call a function with its package name:

tibble::tibble(a = 1)

# A tibble: 1 × 1
      a
  <dbl>
1     1


In this training, we will usually use library() at the start of a script. Short, one-off calls may use ::.
Put the library() calls in your saved code too. A new R session needs to load the packages again.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Meet the tidyverse
The tidyverse is a collection of packages that work well together for common data tasks:


tibble: create and display tables.

dplyr: filter rows, change columns, and summarise data.

readr: read files such as CSVs.

tidyr: reshape tables.

ggplot2: make plots.

We will load the packages we need for each example. The functions often take a table as their first input.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Our first table

library(tibble)

people <- tibble(
  name = c("Alex", "Sam", "Jo"),
  age = c(24, 31, 17),
  group = c("A", "B", "A")
)
people

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  name    age group
  <chr> <dbl> <chr>
1 Alex     24 A    
2 Sam      31 B    
3 Jo       17 A    


Each row describes one person. Each column holds one type of information.
A tibble is a type of data frame. Think of both as tables with named columns.

title: Introduction to R
section: Pick a column or inspect the table
text:
Pick a column or inspect the table

people$age

[1] 24 31 17

mean(people$age)

[1] 24

nrow(people)

[1] 3


$ selects a named column. nrow() counts rows.

names(people)

[1] "name"  "age"   "group"


names() shows column names. This is useful if a later example says that a column cannot be found.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Filter and change a table

library(dplyr)

adults <- filter(people, age >= 18)
adults <- mutate(adults, age_next_year = age + 1)
adults

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  name    age group age_next_year
  <chr> <dbl> <chr>         <dbl>
1 Alex     24 A                25
2 Sam      31 B                32


filter() keeps the rows that match a condition. mutate() creates or changes columns.
Inside these functions, we can write age directly because they look for columns in the supplied table.

title: Introduction to R
Introduction to R
text:
Summarise a table

people |>
  filter(age >= 18) |>
  count(group)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  group     n
  <chr> <int>
1 A         1
2 B         1


Some verbs you will see again:


filter(): keep rows.

select(): keep columns.

mutate(): create or change columns.

summarise(): calculate summaries, such as a mean.

arrange(): sort rows.

title: Introduction to R
text:
The dbplyr package
Our packages use the dbplyr package to translate R code into SQL, the following book should give you the main basis of how our ecosystem of packages work:
https://ohdsi.github.io/Tidy-R-programming-with-OMOP/

title: Introduction to R
text:
Find files with here

library(here)
here()

[1] "/home/runner/work/HDS-OMOP-course/HDS-OMOP-course"


here() finds the project root. We can build paths from it without typing a computer-specific address:

here("data", "data1.csv")

This points to data/data1.csv inside your project. It does not create the file: we will download it in the Quarto session.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Reading a CSV: a preview
A CSV stores a table as plain text. The first line usually contains column names.
After downloading data1.csv in the Quarto session, we can read it with:

library(readr)
library(here)

data <- read_csv(here("data", "data1.csv"))
head(data)

Keep this example for later. read_csv() brings the file into R; head() displays the first few rows.

title: Introduction to R
text:
If something goes wrong


Object not found: check the spelling and run the line that creates the object first.

Could not find function: load its package with library().

No such file: check the active project, folder, filename, and capital letters.

Unexpected symbol: check quotes, commas, and brackets near the reported line.

Start at the first error, fix it, and rerun that part. A message or warning is not always an error; read what it says before moving on.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Ready for the next session
You now have a project, a saved script, and some code you can rerun.
Objects in the Environment belong to the current R session. Your saved script is how you recreate them after restarting R.

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
CodelistGenerator

The CodelistGenerator R package provides tools to


Explore OMOP CDM vocabularies available in the database
Generate codelists systematically using vocabulary-based search strategies
Generate codelist diagnostics to assess code use and identify potentially missing concepts

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Generating candidate concepts
Today, we’ll focus on the getCandidateCodes() function to identify candidate concepts for our two phenotypes.

getCandidateCodes(
  cdm,
  keywords,
  exclude = NULL,
  domains = "Condition",
  vocabularyId = NULL,
  standardConcept = "Standard",
  searchInSynonyms = FALSE,
  searchNonStandard = FALSE,
  includeDescendants = TRUE,
  includeAncestor = FALSE
)


The function returns candidate concepts for review, together with the search strategy used to identify them.
This allows us to define a systematic and reproducible codelist search strategy.

Primary hypertension cohort

We will progressively apply our cohort inclusion criteria to identify adults with primary (essential) hypertension.

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Primary hypertension cohort
→ Apply the inclusion criteria
Now we apply inclusion criteria in a pipeline-fashion to refine the base cohort:

cdm$essential_hypertension <- cdm$essential_hypertension_base |>

  # Age ≥18 and ≥180 days of prior observation
  requireDemographics(
    ageRange = c(18, 150),
    minPriorObservation = 180,
    name = "essential_hypertension"
  ) |>

  # Require another hypertension record within 365 days
  requireCohortIntersect(
    targetCohortTable = "essential_hypertension_base",
    window = c(1, 365),
    intersections = c(1, Inf),
    name = "essential_hypertension"
  ) |>

  # Follow until the end of observation
  exitAtObservationEnd(
    name = "essential_hypertension"
  )

More complex phenotype definitions
Our primary hypertension cohort was a simple example to illustrate the workflow.
We can also implement more complex phenotype definitions combining different types of clinical evidence.

For instance we could use systolic and diastolic blood pressure measurements:

  conceptSet = codelist["systolic_blood_pressure"],
  valueAsNumber = list(c(140, 99999)),
  name = "systolic_blood_pressure"
)

  cdm = cdm, 
  conceptSet = codelist["diastolic_blood_pressure"],
  valueAsNumber = list(c(90, 99999)),

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Warfarin cohort
→ Create treatment episodes and identify new users
We now combine nearby exposures into treatment episodes and apply our new-user criteria:

cdm$warfarin_new_users <- cdm$warfarin_base |>

  # Collapse exposures separated by ≤30 days
  collapseCohorts(
    gap = 30,
    name = "warfarin_new_users"
  ) |>

  # Require ≥365 days of prior observation
  requireDemographics(
    minPriorObservation = 365,
    name = "warfarin_new_users"
  ) |>

  # No warfarin exposure during the previous 365 days
  requireCohortIntersect(
    targetCohortTable = "warfarin_base",

Git vs GitHub vs GitHub Desktop

Git records versions of files on your computer. We can see what changed and return to earlier versions.

Local means on your computer. Remote means the shared copy on GitHub. Saving a file locally does not automatically send it to GitHub.

Repository (Repo)
A repository, or repo, is a folder with Git tracking enabled. It holds the files we choose to track and the history of their committed changes.
An R Project helps RStudio organise your work. A Git repository records its history. A folder can be both, but they do different jobs.

You can use Markdown syntax to format a text file:

# to add a heading.

Public and private repositories

A public repository can be viewed and cloned by anyone, including people without access to our organisation. Only people with the appropriate permission can push changes to it.
A private repository can only be viewed or cloned by people and teams who have been given access. Use this for study code or other work that is not ready to be shared publicly.

Repository visibility is not a safe place for secrets or patient data. Do not commit passwords, access tokens, credentials, or identifiable patient data to either type of repository.

text:
Commit
A commit records a version of the changes you choose to include. Give it a short message so someone else can understand what you did.

Every commit has an ID, an author, a time, and a message.
Commits are created locally with Git.

Push & Pull
These are the actions used to synchronise your local Git repository with the remote repository on GitHub:

Push: Send your committed changes from your computer to the remote repository on GitHub.
Pull: Fetch changes from GitHub and integrate them into your current local branch. We will practise this later.

Issues

An issue is a place to track a task, bug, or idea. It gives the team a place to discuss the work, assign responsibility, and keep track of progress.

Clone means download a repository and its history to your computer. In GitHub Desktop, choose File → Clone Repository… and select your colleague’s repository or paste its URL.

Branch
A branch lets us work on a proposed change before it is added to the main version.

The default and main line of development is typically called the main branch.
In GitHub Desktop, use Current branch → New branch. Name it review_codelist.

Fork
A fork is a copy of a repository in your GitHub account. You can propose changes from it with a pull request when the repository’s permissions allow this.
Because this practice repository is public, anyone can view, clone, or fork it, but public visibility does not give them permission to push changes. For this exercise, we will use write access to each other’s repositories and work on branches.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop

Pull Request (PR)
A pull request (PR) proposes changes from one branch to another, usually so the team can discuss and review them before merging.

PRs are where discussion, code review, and automated testing happen before the code is integrated.

title: OmopViewer
text:
From reports to apps
In Quarto we rendered a report with fixed plots and tables. A Shiny app lets someone interact with the results. They can choose a database, change a filter, or switch between plots, and the displayed output can update.
A Shiny app has a user interface and a server function. We will keep them in separate files, matching the structure that OmopViewer generates:


ui.R defines the ui object: the controls someone can use and the spaces where outputs will appear.

server.R defines the server function that reads those inputs and creates the outputs.

When an input changes, Shiny updates the outputs that depend on it. This is reactivity.
Here, “server” means a function in our R code. Both files form one app, which can run on your own computer.

title: OmopViewer
text:
Your first Shiny app
Reopen practical.Rproj after the OmopStudyBuilder session. In RStudio, choose File → New File → Shiny Web App…, name the app first-shiny, and select a multiple-file app.
Click Run App and move the slider in the starter histogram example. What changes?

RStudio creates first-shiny/ui.R and first-shiny/server.R. Shiny reads both files when it starts the app.
Install shiny and bslib if RStudio reports that either is missing.
The app keeps your R session busy while it runs. Click Stop in RStudio before running other code or restarting the app.

title: OmopViewer
text:
The UI: what goes where?
Replace the contents of first-shiny/ui.R with:

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Hello Shiny!"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      sliderInput("bins", "Number of bins:",
                  min = 1, max = 50, value = 30)
    ),
    mainPanel(plotOutput("distPlot"))
  )
)

bins is the slider’s ID. distPlot is the space where the server will put the plot. These IDs connect the two parts of the app.

title: OmopViewer
text:
The server: make the plot
Replace the contents of first-shiny/server.R with:

library(shiny)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$distPlot <- renderPlot({
    x <- faithful$waiting
    bins <- seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = input$bins + 1)
    hist(x, breaks = bins, col = "steelblue", border = "white",
         xlab = "Waiting time to next eruption (minutes)",
         main = "Old Faithful")
  })
}

faithful is a built-in dataset; the histogram groups its waiting times into bins. input$bins reads the slider, and output$distPlot sends the plot to the UI.
Just as $ picked a table column in R, here it picks a named input or output. renderPlot() reruns when the slider value changes.

title: OmopViewer
section: Give the UI a style with bslib
text:
Give the UI a style with bslib
bslib gives us layouts, cards, sidebars, and themes. Replace the contents of ui.R with this code and leave server.R unchanged:

library(shiny)
library(bslib)

ui <- page_sidebar(
  title = "My first app",
  theme = bs_theme(bootswatch = "flatly"),
  sidebar = sidebar(
    sliderInput("bins", "Number of bins:",
                min = 1, max = 50, value = 30)
  ),
  card(plotOutput("distPlot"))
)

Save ui.R and click Run App again. The IDs still connect the slider in ui.R to the plot created in server.R.

title: OmopViewer
text:
Meet OmopViewer
Building every filter, table, and plot by hand takes time. OmopViewer creates a multiple-file Shiny app for us from supported OMOP study results.
It generates separate UI, server, and setup files. We can then make small changes to fit our study.

Two ways to use it:


launchDynamicApp(): quickly inspect uploaded results without creating an app project.

exportStaticApp(): generate a persistent set of app files that we can inspect, edit, and share.

title: OmopViewer
text:
What data does it need?
OmopViewer works with summarised_result objects: summary estimates together with settings that describe the analyses that produced them.
The settings help OmopViewer choose the appropriate panels for supported result types.

For this exercise, we will use cohort attrition and characteristics results from the reporting training, for amoxicillin and metformin.
Attrition shows how cohort counts change as criteria are applied. Characteristics describe the people in the cohorts, such as their ages. We will learn to produce these results later in the course.
Download OmopViewer results for this exercise. The four-column Data 1 and Data 2 files from the Quarto session are ordinary tables and cannot be used directly here.

Open the dynamic viewer

Upload omopviewer_results.csv, then use Bind data and load shiny to build the panels.

This is a quick way to look at results without creating an app project. Stop the app in RStudio when you want to continue coding.

Import the results in R
Stop the dynamic app and return to omopviewer.R.

library(OmopViewer)
library(omopgenerics)
library(here)
library(shiny)

result <- importSummarisedResult(
  here("data", "omopviewer_results.csv")
)
settings(result)

Use importSummarisedResult() to restore the results and their settings. read_csv() alone does not reconstruct this object.

  directory = here("viewer"),

  open = FALSE

OmopViewer creates a shiny folder inside viewer. Here, “static” means the results are supplied when we generate the app; the app itself is still interactive and needs R to run.

title: OmopViewer
text:
What did OmopViewer create?
Stop the app, then open viewer/shiny in RStudio’s Files pane.
For this exercise, keep practical as the active R Project. Browse the files without opening the generated shiny.Rproj, so the here() paths in our script stay the same.

What to look for

ui.R
Layout, panels, labels, and input controls.


server.R
Code that responds to inputs and builds outputs.


functions.R
Helper functions used by the UI and server.


background.md
Text for the background panel.



rawData/ and data/

Original results, preparation code, and prepared app data.

title: OmopViewer
text:
Start with the export options
Before editing the generated files, try changing the title and hiding the summary panel:

exportStaticApp(
  result = result,
  directory = here("viewer_custom"),
  title = "Exploring our cohorts",
  background = TRUE,
  summary = FALSE,
  open = FALSE

We use a second folder so we can compare the two apps. There are also options for themes, logos, and organising panels.

title: OmopViewer
text:
YOUR TURN Make it yours
Stop the app and work in viewer_custom/shiny:

Edit background.md: add a heading and two sentences explaining what someone can explore.
Open ui.R. Find a visible label and change its text. Keep input and output IDs the same so their connections still work.
Find the corresponding input or output in server.R. Can you follow what it does?
Run the app again and check your changes.


runApp(here("viewer_custom", "shiny"))

Save your edits before restarting. Exporting again to the same location can overwrite the generated app, so use a new folder if you want to keep your manual changes.

title: OmopViewer
section: If the app does not start
text:
If the app does not start


R is still busy: stop the previous app before running more code.

Result object not found: rerun the import step in omopviewer.R.

Cannot find a file: check that practical is still the active project and that you saved the correct CSV in data.

Package missing: install the named package in the active project’s library, then try again.

If a small edit breaks the app, undo that edit and restart. Check labels and IDs carefully; changing the displayed text should not change the connection between UI and server.

title: OmopViewer
section: How does this fit into a study?
text:
How does this fit into a study?
In our exercise, OmopViewer exports to viewer/shiny inside the practice project. OmopStudyBuilder’s studyShiny folder is a place to organise the reporting app for a real study; the tools do not automatically connect these two folders.
Later, the analysis code will produce the summary results that we import here.
Running an app on your computer does not publish it for everyone else. Sharing the app files and hosting an app online are separate steps; deployment is beyond today’s exercise.

title: OmopViewer
text:
Final remarks


Shiny: ui.R collects inputs and displays outputs; server.R connects them with R code.

OmopViewer: creates the app structure and result panels for us.
Use the dynamic viewer to explore, or export an app when you want to customise it.

Start with a small change, run the app, and see what happens :)

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
Why OmopStudyBuilder?
We have seen how an R Project keeps our work together and how GitHub helps us share it. Now imagine several teams running the same study in different OMOP databases.
It helps if everyone knows where to find the code, the instructions, and the results.

OmopStudyBuilder gives us a common starting structure for study projects and repositories. We add the study-specific code and documentation.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
What will we do?

Create the study structure with initStudy().
Explore the generated files and create a private repository on GitHub.
See how renv records the packages a project uses.
Use reviewStudy() to get an overview of the code and dependencies.

The package also has Docker tools for running studies in containers. Today we will focus on setting up and reviewing a study.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
Create a study
Reopen practical.Rproj. Choose a new folder beside it, replacing yourusername with your GitHub username:

library(OmopStudyBuilder)
library(here)

study <- "hds-study-yourusername"
initStudy(
  directory = file.path(dirname(here()), study),
  studyTitle = "My HDS practice study",
  studyLeads = "Your name",
  studyDescription = "Practising a shared OMOP study structure.",
  repository = study,
  organisation = "oxford-pharmacoepi",
  private = TRUE
)

The destination must be new or empty. Let initStudy() create its contents before opening any of the generated R Projects.
dirname(here()) finds the folder containing your current project; file.path() builds the path to the new study folder.
Unlike the first public practice repository, this study repository is private. Only people and teams given access can view or clone it. private = TRUE makes that choice explicit, although it is also the function’s default.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
What did it create?
hds-study-yourusername/
├── README.md
├── INSTRUCTIONS.md
├── diagnosticsCode/
├── diagnosticsShiny/
├── studyCode/
└── studyShiny/


diagnosticsCode: diagnostics of phenotypes.

studyCode: run the study analyses.

diagnosticsShiny and studyShiny: places for apps that explore the results.

Both diagnostics and study default to TRUE. Set either to FALSE in initStudy() if you do not need that pair of folders.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
One repository, several R Projects
Each of the four component folders contains an .Rproj file. Open the project for the part you are working on.
For example, open studyCode/studyCode.Rproj for the main analysis. In that session, here() points to studyCode, not the whole repository.
This still follows our “one project for one piece of work” approach: the repository groups several separate components together.







File or folder inside studyCode

What goes there?



codeToRun.R
The entry script, including database-specific settings.


runStudy.R
The sequence of study steps.



codelist/ and cohorts/

Code to define the study population.


analyses/
Code for the analyses.


Results/
Output from the study.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
YOUR TURN Explore the template

Run the initStudy() example with your own folder name and study details.
Read the root README.md and INSTRUCTIONS.md. Which parts would you update for a real study?
Open studyCode/studyCode.Rproj, then look at codeToRun.R and runStudy.R.
Find where you would add cohort definitions and an analysis.

For now, explore the scripts rather than sourcing them: the database connection and study-specific code are still to be filled in.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
section: YOUR TURN Link the repository to GitHub Desktop
text:
YOUR TURN Link the repository to GitHub Desktop

Check that the repo exists online and is labelled Private.
Link it to GitHub desktop with the option Add... -> Add existing repository

title: OmopStudyBuilder
section: Keep the instructions with the code
text:
Keep the instructions with the code
In the root README, write a short description of your practice study. For example: which population would you study, and what would you measure?
Then use the workflow from the GitHub session:

Create a branch for your changes.
Commit and push them.
Open a pull request and ask a colleague whether the instructions are clear.

After merging, switch to main in Desktop and Fetch origin → Pull origin to update your local copy.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
Why use renv?
The same code can behave differently when people have different package versions. renv gives an R Project its own package library and records package versions in renv.lock.


The study developer prepares the environment and records it.
A colleague restores that environment when they run the study.
The lockfile is committed alongside the code, so changes can be reviewed in GitHub.

The generated study folders do not yet contain a lockfile. Prepare renv in each component R Project that you use, after deciding which packages its code needs.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
renv: the basic workflow (demo)
Watch this first; setting up the full template’s packages can take time. Open studyCode/studyCode.Rproj, install renv if needed, and initialise it once:

install.packages("renv")
library(renv)
init()

init() scans the project and prepares its package library and lockfile. It may need to install packages referenced by the template.






Function
When would we use it?



snapshot()
Record the package versions after changing and checking the code.


restore()
Install the versions recorded in an existing lockfile.


status()
Check whether the project library and lockfile agree.


activate()
Activate renv in a project.


deactivate()
Deactivate renv in a project.



Commit renv.lock and the activation files created by renv; its .gitignore excludes the local package library. renv records the R version but does not install R itself.
More detail: Introduction to renv.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
Get an overview with reviewStudy()
Before sharing code with a data partner, it is useful to see what is in the project.
From the studyCode R Project, install OmopStudyBuilder there if it is missing from your new renv library, then run:

library(OmopStudyBuilder)
library(here)

reviewStudy(dir = here(), dependencies = FALSE)

This prints a summary of the R scripts and JSON, CSV, and Excel files. dependencies = FALSE lets everyone try it, including those who have not set up renv yet.
It gives us a starting point for review; we still need to read the code and check that it answers the study question.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
Review the dependencies too
Once studyCode/renv.lock exists, run:

reviewStudy(dir = here(), type = "analysis")

By default, both code and dependencies are TRUE. The dependency review uses the lockfile and reports on package versions and sources.

For a reporting or app project, open that component’s R Project and use type = "reporting".
Run the review in the component folder containing the lockfile. A review of the repository root will not automatically review every component’s environment.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
YOUR TURN Review your study

Run reviewStudy(dir = here(), dependencies = FALSE) from studyCode.
Find the entry script and the analysis scripts in the output. Which are still empty?
If you have prepared a lockfile, run the dependency review too. Pick one package and find its recorded version.
Add a note to your pull request, or a new issue if it has already been merged, describing what still needs to be completed before the study can run.

Discuss the review with your colleague. A common folder structure makes it easier to find things, but the code and instructions still need a human review.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
Final remarks

Start with initStudy() so everyone recognises the study layout.
Keep the instructions and code together in GitHub.
Use renv to record and restore package versions.
Use reviewStudy() to help you inspect the project before sharing it.

Next, we will see how OmopViewer helps us build apps to explore study results. Reopen practical.Rproj for that exercise so we use the same practice project and data folder as in Quarto.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Quarto
Quarto is a free tool for creating documents from a plain-text source file. You can combine writing, code, and the results of that code in one place.
Use the same source to create reports, presentations, websites, and more. Quarto works with R, Python, Julia, and Observable.
We will use R and return to the practical project. By the end, you will have a report that updates when we replace its input data.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
What happens when you render?
You write your content in a .qmd file. When you render it, Quarto runs the code, adds its output to your writing, and creates the finished document.
That makes it easier to update a report when the data changes: update the data, render again, and the numbers and figures are refreshed from the code.

title: Introduction to Quarto
section: How to create a Quarto document
text:
How to create a Quarto document
Open practical.Rproj. In RStudio, choose File → New File → Quarto Document….
Choose HTML, give it a title, and save it as my-report.qmd in the project root, beside practice.R. Use the Source editor when typing the Markdown examples below.
If the Quarto option is missing or RStudio asks to install a required package, ask for help before continuing.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text: Create a Quarto document

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Choose a format and render
Start with HTML and click Render. Quarto will create a document you can open in your browser.

Render the starter document first. This checks that your setup works.
Then try Word by changing the YAML format to docx and rendering again.
PDF is optional: its usual LaTeX engine needs an extra installation. We can use HTML or Word for all the core exercises.


The writing and code stay in the .qmd source. You can render it again whenever you update the content or data.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Which file do I edit?


my-report.qmd: your editable source, containing writing and code.

my-report.html or my-report.docx: the output created by Render.

Make changes in the .qmd file and render again. Changes made only in the output will not be carried back into your source.
Save my-report.qmd before rendering. Keep the setup and analysis code in the document so someone else can recreate the report.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Parts of a Quarto document
A .qmd file has two main parts:


Metadata at the top, between lines containing ---. This is YAML and stores settings such as the title and output format.

Document body below the metadata. This contains your text, headings, code, and other content to render.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Write some text
This is the same Markdown we used in GitHub’s README. For example:
# Main heading
## Smaller heading

This is a paragraph with **bold text**.

- This is a list item.
- And another one.

Render the document and see how the source becomes a formatted page.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Add some code
Use RStudio’s Insert Code Chunk control to insert an R chunk. Paste this code inside it, then render:

scores <- c(7, 8, 10)
mean(scores)

[1] 8.333333



The code and its result are connected: change the values and render again to update the result.

title: Introduction to Quarto
section: What does a chunk look like?
text:
What does a chunk look like?
In the Source editor, an executable R chunk has an opening line, the R code, and a closing line:
```{r}
scores <- c(7, 8, 10)
mean(scores)
```
The three backticks mark the boundaries. {r} says to run the contents as R code. Ordinary writing goes outside the chunk.
You can use the chunk’s green arrow to try it, but Render rebuilds the whole document.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
echo, eval, message, and warning

These options control what happens to code chunks:


echo: show (TRUE) or hide (FALSE) the code in the rendered document.

eval: run (TRUE) or skip (FALSE) the code.

message and warning: show or hide messages and warnings produced by the code.


Set options in the chunk header. For example, this runs the summary and shows its result while hiding its code and messages:
```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
summary(scores)
```
Use echo=FALSE when you want results without the code. eval=FALSE means the code will not run, so it cannot create objects for later chunks.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Set defaults for the document

Add an execute: section to the YAML at the top of your document. These defaults run the code but hide it in the output:
---
execute:
  echo: false
  eval: true
---
Keep your existing title and format. Add these options inside the same YAML block, keeping the indentation shown above. Individual chunks can override the defaults.

title: Introduction to Quarto
section: Render starts a fresh R session
text:
Render starts a fresh R session
When you click Render, Quarto runs your document from the top in a fresh session. Objects you created only in the Console are not automatically available.
Include the library() calls, file-reading code, and calculations in your .qmd file, in the order they are needed.
If you see object not found, look for the earlier chunk that should create it. Check that it runs and that the object name is the same in both places.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
YOUR TURN Get the data

Open the course website’s Downloads tab and choose your GitHub username.
Click Download Data 1 results and save data1.csv in practical/data.
Read it into your Quarto document. Add a sentence, table, or plot that tells us something about the data.

These are made-up prevalence percentages for five conditions. Each row describes a database, condition, year, and prevalence. For example, 8.4 means 8.4%.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Read and inspect the data
In my-report.qmd, add an R chunk and paste this code. Keep it above the chunks that use data:

library(readr)
library(here)

data <- read_csv(here("data", "data1.csv"))
head(data)

Render and check the column names. If the file cannot be found, check its name and make sure it is in this project’s data folder.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Find a value to describe
Add another R chunk below the data-reading chunk. Here we find the row with the highest prevalence across all years and databases:

library(dplyr)

highest_example <- data |>
  filter(prevalence == max(prevalence))
highest_example

max() finds the largest value; filter() keeps matching rows. This example dataset has one highest row. With other data, ties could give us several rows.

title: Introduction to Quarto
section: Put a result inside a sentence
text:
Put a result inside a sentence
Below the previous chunk, paste this sentence as ordinary document text. The expressions between backticks are inline R:
The highest prevalence is `r highest_example$prevalence`%
for `r highest_example$condition`
in `r highest_example$database` in `r highest_example$year`.
Render the document. Quarto replaces each inline expression with its value, so the text updates with the data too.
Here, $ selects a column from highest_example, just as we used people$age in the R session.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Add a plot
Add one more R chunk:

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data, aes(x = year, y = prevalence, colour = condition)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~database) +
  labs(y = "Prevalence (%)")

As before, aes() connects columns to the axes and colours. facet_wrap() creates a separate panel for each database.
YOUR TURN: change the plot title or hide the code with echo=FALSE, then render again.

Spacing in Quarto
Leave a blank line in the source to start a new paragraph. Extra empty lines in the source do not add extra space in the output.
To add a blank line in your Word report, put   (a non-breaking space) on its own line, with a blank line before and after it:
Text before a blank line.

To insert a page break in Word, put this shortcode on its own line, with a blank line before and after it:
Text before the page break.

{{< pagebreak >}}

Text on the next page.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Optional: use a Word template
A template gives documents a shared look and saves you from formatting every report by hand. For a Word report, a reference document can define headings, fonts, spacing, headers, footers, and caption styles.
Quarto uses the content and styles in your .qmd file; Word uses the matching styles in the reference document to decide how those parts look.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Example of a Word template
The darwinReportRef.docx template is an example of a Word reference document.
On GitHub, use Download raw file to save the .docx file, then open it in Word to explore the styles. Save it beside my-report.qmd.
Replace your existing format: setting in the YAML with:
format:
  docx:
    reference-doc: "darwinReportRef.docx"

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Custom styles for captions
You can give a block of text a style name that exists in the Word reference document:
:::{custom-style="FigureCaption"}
Figure 1. Prevalence of the different conditions over time.
:::

:::{custom-style="CaptionFooter"}
CI = confidence interval
:::
Create or change the FigureCaption and CaptionFooter styles in the Word template to control their appearance. The style names in the document and template need to match.

A new partner, SIDI Or, sends results at the last minute. SIDI Plata updates its results, while SIDI Bronze stays the same. Let’s refresh our report:

title: Introduction to Quarto
section: If the report does not render
text:
If the report does not render


Object or function not found: include the data-reading code and library() calls in the document, above the analysis.

File not found: check the active project, the data folder, and the exact filename.

YAML error: check spaces and indentation at the top. Do not add a second format: key.

PDF/LaTeX error: continue with HTML or Word. PDF setup is optional today; see the Quarto PDF guide.

Fix the first reported error and render again. Ask for help if the message does not make sense.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Final remarks

Keep the writing, code, and results together in the .qmd source.
Use a template when reports need a consistent look.
When the data changes, update the input files and render again.


That’s Quarto: write it once, render it when you need it, and let the code update the results.
Save my-report.qmd in practical. Next, OmopStudyBuilder will help us organise a bigger study into a shared repository.

What you will be able to do

Add patient-level characteristics to cohort and CDM tables.
Check whether records are inside observation and quantify lookback/follow-up time.
Create features from intersections with cohorts, concepts, and OMOP CDM tables.

title: PatientProfiles

Today’s workflow

Connect to a synthetic OMOP CDM database.
Create two small cohorts for live examples.
Add demographics and observation-period features.
Build intersection features.

title: PatientProfiles
text:
Settings

PatientProfiles starts with a table that has a person identifier and, usually, an index date.


It returns the same table with extra columns.








Tip


For cohort tables, the default index date is cohort_start_date. For CDM clinical tables, set the relevant date column explicitly.

Load the required packages



library(PatientProfiles)

cdm <- omock::mockCdmFromDataset(source = "duckdb", datasetName = "synpuf-1k" )

  conceptSet = list(arthritis = c(80180, 80809)),

text:
Introduction

CohortConstructor package is designed to support cohort building pipelines in R, using data mapped to the OMOP Common Data Model.





The code is publicly available in OHDSI’s GitHub repository CohortConstructor.





CohortConstructor v0.6.3 is available in CRAN.





Vignettes with further information can be found in the package website.

title: CohortConstructor
text:
OMOP Cohorts in R

The <cohort_table> class is defined in the R package omopgenerics.
This is the class that CohortConstructor uses, as well as other OMOP analytical packages.

As defined in omopgenerics, a <cohort_table> must have at least the following 4 columns (without any missing values in them):

cohort_definition_id: Unique identifier for each cohort in the table.
subject_id: Unique patient identifier.
cohort_start_date: Date when the person enters the cohort.
cohort_end_date: Date when the person exits the cohort.

title: Welcome
text:
Welcome
Welcome to the HDS OMOP training! We will write some code, share it with each other, and use it to explore study results.
You do not need to know every tool already. We will build things step by step, and there will be time to try them yourself.
Tell us your name, what you work on, and whether you have used R or GitHub before.

title: Welcome
text:
What are we working towards?


Day 1: get comfortable with the tools for writing, sharing, and reporting our work.

Day 2: define study populations with codelists and cohorts, then check them using synthetic data.

Day 3: describe the people in those cohorts and explore their characteristics.

Today we will work with practice files and supplied results. You do not need a connection to a patient database for the Day 1 exercises.

title: Welcome
section: A few words we will use
text:
A few words we will use






Word
What we mean today



OMOP CDM
A common structure and vocabulary for health data, so the same analysis can be adapted across databases.


Codelist
A list of concept IDs used to identify something, such as a condition or a medicine.


Cohort
A group of people who meet a definition, with dates describing their membership.


Network study
Several data partners running a shared study in their own databases.



We will spend more time on OMOP, concepts, and cohort definitions on Day 2. For today, these are the examples we will use while learning the tools.

text:
How Day 1 fits together






Session
What you will practise



R
Save a script, work with a small table, and make a plot.


GitHub
Share a file, review a colleague’s changes, and merge them.


Quarto
Turn code and results into a report that you can update.


OmopStudyBuilder
Create a study repository with a recognisable structure.


OmopViewer
Explore results in an app and make a small change to it.



Each session adds something to the previous one. Keep the files you create so you can return to them later.
